This vignette uses the National Supported Work Demonstration (NSW)
job-training data distributed through the `causaldata` example-data package and
mirrored by
[RDatasets](https://vincentarelbundock.github.io/Rdatasets/doc/causaldata/nsw_mixtape.html).
NSW was a large social experiment from the 1970s that targeted disadvantaged
workers. Treated participants were offered a supported work placement for a
limited period, and later earnings were measured from administrative records.

The causal question is:

```text
What is the effect of job-training participation on real earnings in 1978?
```

The example is useful because the same economic question can be represented by
several graphs:

1. an experimental graph, where assignment is treated as randomized;
2. an observational selection-on-observables graph, where baseline covariates
   confound participation and later earnings;
3. a sensitivity graph with unmeasured selection, where the effect is no longer
   identified by the implemented criteria.

The research idea is the classic program-evaluation problem: can an employment
and training program raise later earnings? NSW is especially useful because it
connects an experimental benchmark to the observational problem economists
often face. If assignment is randomized, a simple comparison can estimate the
effect. If participation is analyzed as if it came from a non-random labor
market or administrative process, baseline earnings, education, age, race,
marital status, and degree status become part of the identifying story. The
DAG makes those alternative stories explicit before estimation.

## Setup

```{julia}
import Pkg
Pkg.activate(joinpath(@__DIR__, ".."); io=devnull)

using CausalGraphs
using DataFrames
using DelimitedFiles
using Downloads
using Printf
using Statistics
```

## 1. Load NSW Data

The treatment is `treat`, an indicator for participation in the job-training
program. The outcome is `re78`, real earnings in 1978. The baseline variables
are demographic characteristics and pre-treatment earnings in 1974 and 1975.
The RDatasets file used here has 445 observations and 11 variables. The
analysis below keeps the variables needed for the treatment, outcome, and
baseline adjustment set.

```{julia}
function read_rdatasets_csv(url, cols)
    local_file = Downloads.download(url; timeout=120)
    x, header = readdlm(local_file, ',', Any, '\n'; header=true)
    raw = DataFrame(x, Symbol.(vec(header)))
    DataFrame((c => Float64.(raw[!, c]) for c in cols)...)
end

url = "https://vincentarelbundock.github.io/Rdatasets/csv/causaldata/nsw_mixtape.csv"

cols = [
    :treat, :age, :educ, :black, :hisp, :marr, :nodegree,
    :re74, :re75, :re78,
]

data = read_rdatasets_csv(url, cols);

println("n = ", nrow(data))
println("treated = ", Int(sum(data.treat .== 1)))
println("controls = ", Int(sum(data.treat .== 0)))
first(data, 5)
```

This version of the data contains treated and control units from the NSW
experiment. RDatasets also provides observational comparison samples, such as
the Current Population Survey counterpart. We start with the experimental
sample because it gives a clear baseline for the graph-based workflow.

## 2. Experimental Graph

In the randomized interpretation of the NSW experiment, assignment to training
is not caused by baseline earnings, education, age, or other participant
characteristics. The graph for the average effect of training on later earnings
is therefore simple:

```text
A -> Y
```

where `A` is program participation and `Y` is real earnings in 1978.

```{julia}
experimental_graph = make_graph(
    vertices = [:treat, :re78],
    di_edges = [(:treat, :re78)],
);
```

```{julia}
#| output: asis
println("```{mermaid}")
println(to_mermaid(experimental_graph; direction="LR"))
println("```")
```

Identification is immediate. The Markov pillow of the treatment is empty, so
the estimator does not adjust for baseline covariates.

```{julia}
experimental_id = identify(experimental_graph, :treat, :re78)
println("strategy: ", experimental_id.strategy)
println("Markov pillow of treat: ",
        markov_pillow(experimental_graph, :treat; treatment=:treat))
```

```{julia}
raw_difference = mean(data.re78[data.treat .== 1]) -
                 mean(data.re78[data.treat .== 0])

experimental_res = estimate_causal(
    a = [1, 0],
    data = select(data, [:treat, :re78]),
    graph = experimental_graph,
    treatment = :treat,
    outcome = :re78,
);

@printf("Raw difference in means: %.2f\n", raw_difference)
@printf("TMLE: ACE = %.2f  95%% CI (%.2f, %.2f)\n",
        experimental_res[:TMLE].ACE,
        experimental_res[:TMLE].lower_ci,
        experimental_res[:TMLE].upper_ci)
```

In this simple randomized graph, the TMLE estimate is essentially the difference
in sample means. The graph records the strong identifying assumption: treatment
assignment is independent of potential earnings.

## 3. Observational Selection Graph

Suppose instead that we are analyzing a non-random comparison between trainees
and non-trainees. Then baseline characteristics may affect both program
participation and later earnings. A compact conceptual graph is:

```text
X -> A -> Y
X -----> Y
```

Here `X` contains baseline age, education, race/ethnicity indicators, marital
status, degree status, and pre-treatment earnings.

```{julia}
conceptual_graph = make_graph(
    vertices = [:X, :A, :Y],
    di_edges = [(:X, :A), (:X, :Y), (:A, :Y)],
);
```

```{julia}
#| output: asis
println("```{mermaid}")
println(to_mermaid(conceptual_graph; direction="LR"))
println("```")
```

For estimation, the grouped node `X` is expanded into the actual data columns.

```{julia}
vertices = [
    :age, :educ, :black, :hisp, :marr, :nodegree,
    :re74, :re75, :treat, :re78,
]

baseline = setdiff(vertices, [:treat, :re78])

edges = vcat(
    [(w, :treat) for w in baseline],
    [(w, :re78) for w in baseline],
    [(:treat, :re78)],
)

observational_graph = make_graph(vertices=vertices, di_edges=edges);
```

```{julia}
#| output: asis
println("```{mermaid}")
println(to_mermaid(observational_graph; direction="LR"))
println("```")
```

Under this graph, the effect is identified by adjustment for the measured
baseline variables.

```{julia}
observational_id = identify(observational_graph, :treat, :re78)
println("strategy: ", observational_id.strategy)
println("Markov pillow of treat: ",
        markov_pillow(observational_graph, :treat; treatment=:treat))
```

```{julia}
observational_res = estimate_causal(
    a = [1, 0],
    data = data,
    graph = observational_graph,
    treatment = :treat,
    outcome = :re78,
);

@printf("TMLE:    ACE = %.2f  95%% CI (%.2f, %.2f)\n",
        observational_res[:TMLE].ACE,
        observational_res[:TMLE].lower_ci,
        observational_res[:TMLE].upper_ci)
@printf("Onestep: ACE = %.2f\n", observational_res[:Onestep].ACE)
@printf("Gcomp:   ACE = %.2f\n", observational_res[:Gcomp].ACE)
@printf("IPW:     ACE = %.2f\n", observational_res[:IPW].ACE)
```

This adjusted estimate answers a different identifying story than the
experimental estimate. It is the effect under the assumption that the listed
baseline variables block all backdoor paths from training to 1978 earnings.

## 4. Sensitivity to Unmeasured Selection

In many economic applications, selection into training may depend on factors not
recorded in the data: motivation, caseworker discretion, informal job networks,
local labor-market opportunity, or health. A compact way to represent that
concern is a bidirected edge between training and later earnings:

```text
X -> A -> Y
X -----> Y
A <-> Y
```

The bidirected edge says that `A` and `Y` share an unmeasured common cause after
conditioning on the measured baseline variables.

```{julia}
selection_graph = make_graph(
    vertices = vertices,
    di_edges = edges,
    bi_edges = [(:treat, :re78)],
);
```

```{julia}
#| output: asis
println("```{mermaid}")
println(to_mermaid(selection_graph; direction="LR"))
println("```")
```

```{julia}
selection_id = identify(selection_graph, :treat, :re78)
println("strategy with unmeasured selection: ", selection_id.strategy)
```

With this additional unmeasured-confounding assumption, `CausalGraphs.jl`
reports the effect as not identified. That is the main lesson of the example:
the identifying conclusion is conditional on the graph, and a substantively
plausible change in the graph can change whether estimation is justified.

## 5. Optional Observational Counterpart

The same graph can be used with an observational comparison sample, such as the
RDatasets `cps_mixtape` file. That dataset contains CPS nonparticipants as an
observational control group for the NSW treated units. Running the same
adjustment graph there is reasonable only under the stronger selection-on-
observables assumption encoded above.

```{julia}
#| eval: false
cps_url = "https://vincentarelbundock.github.io/Rdatasets/csv/causaldata/cps_mixtape.csv"
cps_data = read_rdatasets_csv(cps_url, cols)

cps_res = estimate_causal(
    a = [1, 0],
    data = cps_data,
    graph = observational_graph,
    treatment = :treat,
    outcome = :re78,
)
```

This optional extension is deliberately not the default estimate in the
vignette. The point is to separate the graph for an experimental sample from
the stronger graph required for an observational comparison.

## Summary

This example shows an applied economics workflow:

1. Draw the graph for the design or identifying assumption.
2. Run `identify()` before estimating.
3. Estimate only under graphs where the effect is identified.
4. Compare candidate graphs to make identifying assumptions explicit.

For the NSW data, the experimental graph and the measured-confounding graph both
route to `:a_fixable`. Adding an unmeasured common cause of training and
earnings changes the route to `:not_identified`.
